subject: Edge visibility export schema & SIEM normalization checklist
messages:

Cc: security@acmehealth.com

Subject: Observability exports for on-prem Edge — format and normalization questions

Hi Kimberly / Lauren,

We kicked off the internal SIEM POC this week and have a couple of specific asks before the on-site network review next month:

- Can you confirm the supported output formats for private deployments (syslog RFC5424, Splunk HEC, and HTTPS JSON over mTLS)? Our SIEM team prefers HEC but the network team is pushing syslog over a forwarder.
- Do you provide a canonical field mapping (event schema) or a normalization layer we should expect? For example, mapping of model_id, request_id, customer_id, and redaction flags.
- Tracing hooks: what headers and sampling fields do you emit so we can correlate tokens and user request traces with our APM?
- Any known throughput/cost trade-offs when using HEC vs batched syslog over TLS (we intend to keep retention in our Splunk indexers minimal during POC).

I've attached our initial SIEM requirements sheet with some sample logs. Happy to walk through this on Thursday if that works.

Thanks,
Jorge Alvarez
Engineering Manager, Platform
Acme Health

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Jorge Alvarez <jorge@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-09-07T16:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Observability exports for on-prem Edge — format and normalization questions

Hi Jorge — thanks for the clear list. Short answers up front, then a proposed next step.

1) Supported outputs: we support syslog (RFC5424), Splunk HEC, and HTTPS JSON POST over mTLS. Default connector in VPC build is an adaptable forwarder that can emit any of these.

2) Canonical schema: we maintain a published "visibility schema" that normalizes model_id, request_id, session_id, customer_id, verbatim_tokens (nullable), and a redaction_mask (bitstring). I attached the connector spec that includes the mapping and sample events. The normalization happens in the connector; you can choose to deliver raw events or normalized events to your SIEM.

3) Tracing hooks: we emit: x-rw-request-id, x-rw-span-id, x-traceparent when available, and a sampled flag (rw-sampled: 0/1). For token-level correlation we also attach a per-response kv.cache_id header when cache was used.

4) Throughput/cost: HEC is generally more CPU-bound on our side (JSON parsing and batching) and better for structured events and field extraction. Syslog is lighter-weight but less structured — you usually push a small forwarder that converts syslog into indexed fields in Splunk. If you need field-based alerts during POC, HEC reduces work in Splunk but increases egress bandwidth and connector CPU.

Next step: Marcus (cc'd) can outline an acceptance checklist and recommended handshake ports, and Priyom can run through the runbook for the on-site handoff. I'll open a support ticket and share the runbook and the connector spec now.

Regards,
Kimberly Park
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Attachments: redwood-vpc-obsv-connector-spec.pdf (diagram + schema)

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
To: Jorge Alvarez <jorge@acmehealth.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>, Priyom Das <priyom_das@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-09-08T08:04:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Observability exports for on-prem Edge — acceptance checklist and networking notes

Thanks — adding details you can hand to your SIEM and network teams. Notes below are specific to our private (VPC/on-prem) connector deployment.

Connector modes and tradeoffs:
- HEC (preferred for fielded POC): Sends batched JSON with explicit field mappings. Uses persistent HTTP/1.1 connections and supports token-based auth or mTLS. Pros: easy field extraction, smaller number of events (batched), predictable schema. Cons: higher CPU on connector and higher egress bandwidth for verbose payloads. Expect 10-20% higher egress vs compressed syslog for similar telemetry volume.
- Syslog RFC5424: Emits compact messages suitable for existing log pipelines. Good if you already have a forwarder (syslog-ng/rsyslog) and prefer minimal connector work. Cons: field extraction moves to Splunk/Graylog; correlation keys must be parsable (we include a JSON blob in the message tail for richer fields).
- HTTPS JSON over mTLS: Hybrid approach for trace payloads and higher-priority events. Use this for spans and high-cardinality traces where you want strict delivery guarantees.

Recommended ports/routing:
- Outbound from connector to your SIEM: 443 for HEC/mTLS (destination: your internal HEC endpoint), 6514 for syslog over TLS.
- Allow persistent connections and idle timeouts >= 15m for batching efficiency.
- If using a forwarder cluster, ensure sticky routing from connector instances to a small set of forwarders to preserve request_id ordering for dedup/aggregation.

Event schema & normalization guidance:
- Field names (canonical): rw.model_id, rw.request_id, rw.customer_id, rw.session_id, rw.redaction_mask, rw.latency_ms, rw.kv_cache_hit (boolean).
- We recommend indexing rw.request_id as a keyword/string in Splunk to join traces and logs.
- For PII: our connector will apply configured redaction profiles. The redaction_mask is bit-encoded per-field; we include a human-readable summary in metadata for acceptance testing.

Tracing specifics:
- We emit x-rw-request-id on every top-level event and x-traceparent for W3C trace compatibility. Sampling is controlled at connector level; default sample rate 1% for token-level spans, adjustable per-customer.
- To correlate logs to spans, use rw.request_id + x-traceparent. If you need token-level granularity, enable "detail_spans" in the connector config (note: increases event volume).

Acceptance checklist (minimal for POC):
1) Confirm SIEM endpoint (HEC URL or syslog FQDN) and credentials/cert bundle.
2) Network rules: outbound 443 or 6514 (TLS), and allow sticky NAT for connection pooling.
3) Test dataset: send 5k events with sample traces and verify request_id joins in Splunk within 60s.
4) Redaction validation: provide 10 sample PII-containing requests to validate redaction_mask output.
5) Latency/throughput: validate that connector keeps tail latency < 150 ms for event emission under your expected qps.

I've put these items into a short runbook we can run through on-site. Also linking the connector spec Kimberly attached (same Drive folder).

—Marcus
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
